reviews.text: [i] I'm a simple person, I see dragons, I hit like. None Shall Intrude is a roguelite deck builder that where you are the final raid boss. With element-based combat offering plenty of build variety, and unique additions like a three phase boss mechanic, it creates a fresh and challenging experience. While it starts slow and has a few questionable design choices, it ultimately delivers an enjoyable and distinctive deck-building experience. [/i] [h1]📝 Main Pros, Cons, and Suggestions, followed by the Review:[/h1] 🟩 Pros: + The concept is interesting + Some backdrops (such as the ship) are fun + You play as the boss (dragon) rather than the heroes + The 3 phase boss mechanics are interesting (as you lose HP, you get stronger via new mechanics) + The roguelike aspects revolve around an interesting albeit small talent tree and different boss phase aspects + Build variety offers enough experimentation, creating a lot of interesting interactions between the elements (buff, debuff, aoe etc) 🟥 Cons: - Repetitive tutorial music - Fights are too long (early on) - Mystery reward questions are boring - Harder nodes don't offer better rewards - Lack of sound effects make abilities feel unimpactful - The music is far too intense and repetitive, especially compared to the action - Micro delay in actioning certain moves (not lag, but the animations simply stop for a second) 🏷️ Suggestions: ~ Beastiary ~ Custom death animations ~ Let us play as different bosses ~ Explain card patterns in the tutorial ~ Preview of combo effects when you hover ability over terrain ~ Option for click > click instead of click > drag for playing cards (accessibility) ~ Replace mystery rewards with random RNG buffs or curses, or more creative questions ~ Reference card in the top right shows all combination effects, explain this in the tutorial [h1] While you are a boss, you don’t feel like the boss [/h1] None Shall Intrude (NSI) is a roguelite deck builder where you play as the final raid boss in a 20-stage adventure. Progression has you capturing nodes on the map to unlock unique rewards, facing off against a raid party every five stages, with the ultimate challenge being a battle against the hero in the final stage. While the concept is fresh and engaging, some questionable design choices hold the game back from reaching its full potential. The first questionable design choice comes with the maps node system. Some nodes are marked as harder, but their rewards don’t always reflect the increased difficulty, making the easier nodes the more logical choice. Combat also feels inconsistent, with some elements not fully balancing out, leading to mixed experiences. Combat in NSI revolves around three elements – Fire, earth, and wind – Each having unique interactions with map tiles and between themselves e.g. A fire spell chars a tile, and wind can spread the burn to nearby tiles. At its core, fire deals damage, wind moves enemies, and earth provides armour. The dragon boss theme is also reflected in the inhale/exhale and three phase mechanics, adding extra layers of strategy – These are a nice touch. Where combat falls short however is in the early game, where enemy health pools and numbers feel too large and card damage and variety are lacking, leading to an unsatisfying opening. However, as you unlock buffs, the gameplay becomes more enjoyable, allowing you to clear enemies and boss alternates with ease. While the elements’ interactions with both enemies and terrain add a layer of strategy, wind feels noticeably weaker compared to the other elements, creating an imbalance that detracts from the overall experience. Overall, NSI has a strong foundation and a brilliant concept – Playing as the raid boss is a unique and enjoyable twist. However, the world feels underwhelming, and the execution is average, hindered by several questionable design choices. While it's far from a bad game, it doesn’t seem to offer the same lasting appeal or depth as other titles in the genre – It’s a fun experience, but one that may not hold your attention long-term. Not without its flaws, but if you think you'll enjoy it, you will. Believe it or not, someone with "Dragon" in their name might be biased towards a game where you play as a dragon. Shocker, I know. But regardless of said bias I do think the gameplay itself is really well done. There is a wide variety of builds you can go for, with a bit less randomness than in most deck builders, while still providing incentives to try out different strategies. I heavily enjoy tying achievement to in-game buffs, requiring you to complete a challenge as a sort of "rite of passage" of obtaining a powerful boss mechanic, which can then be crucial to a destructive build. The elemental mechanics are also a really good mix of useful when you're starting of, and really powerful once you get a hang of them, with the order of attacks often strongly impacted by their elemental effects. That being said, it's not all fire and brimstone. While the gameplay itself is really well done, the surrounding gameplay experience is more of a medium-rare, and that's not good when dealing with flying creatures like dragons. It's not that things are bad, but it feels like it's not living up to its potential at times. VFX are wonderful, but SFX feels lacking here and there. Phase transition for bosses are great gameplay-wise, but also slightly underwhelming in how they happen. And while I love the concept of the dragon cave, it feels like there could be so much more done with it, and that it should've been unlocked earlier in the game. I'm sure a lot of things will be improved as updates happen, and feedback/suggestions from players roll in. The devs have had a very rapid pace of updates in the beta period, so fingers crossed for everything to be ironed out within a month of release. If you're on the fence and here around release time, it might be worth waiting a bit to experience the game at its best a few patches from now. But if a slightly imperfect experience sounds like something you can overlook, then the actual game that's underneath is really, really good.

This is one of those games where it could use a "Maybe" review. It is NOT a bad game, but it really feels incomplete at this time. There's also some annoying bugs that affect the game play and some quality of life things too. Some of these issues make it almost feel like a mobile game ported to pc, which to me isn't great. It doesn't feel like a fully baked game, and although I'm hopeful that it will be continued to be worked on, I feel that it's maybe equally likely that it was pushed out for funds. One of the irritating things about this game is that when it comes to manipulating the environment/tiles there isn't any handy previews of what various interactions do or projected damage or anything like that, so if you haven't memorized all of the elemental interactions, there's more guessing than necessary. Since this game does require lite strategy, it really should be easier to tell how you should be trying to set up the board for various combos and whatnot. Or there should be an option to do that. The mechanic where you get to destroy houses is a bit buggy. It will lock you in where you can't end your turn, and that requires a game restart to fix and on top of that the board typically is not exactly as you left. It's frustrating. There is also an issue with easily being able to see the preview of what areas you'll be affecting with your attacks. The models of the buildings can block the marked areas and make it unclear. The reward system has been broken for me as well, especially during the above mentioned encounters. Sometimes you won't get all your rewards and be booted before you can take all of them. It is unclear if this is by design, I have not noticed any clear designations for when it is that you'll be getting all the rewards or when you'll click to select them and have the others disappear. There is also no way to back out of the card choosing, so if you're in a situation where your cards would be withheld, once you click on them to check what your options are, you have to choose one or skip entirely, and if you skip you might lose the other rewards. An example of a better system is how slay the spire offers rewards to players. I shouldn't have to be worried about mis-clicking. It would be nice if there was an endless mode or something where we could take over the entire region. I unexpectedly defeated the final boss and reached the end of the game when I was still looking forward to taking over the 80% of the land that was still free for the taking. Given that the game is so short right now, there isn't much replay value imo currently. It was a let down to beat the guy and then be at the end credits when there seemed like there was much more left to do. Let me be a dragon and go do more dragon things! Granted maybe I'm playing the game wrong, but even then it's not clear if that's the case. Frankly it's a dragon game, so to me that means there should be some god tier type things. Or else what is the point of it being a dragon if we're going to be hamstrung and restricted from burning it all down, building a huge hoard, or other dragon related things? The trailers feel a tad misleading that you can't actually take over everything. Next, it's a bit odd that there are a lot of the identical heroes guarding multiple pieces of territory. I think named heroes are more special when you encounter them, kill them (or not) and then that's the end of them. It feels kind of bizarre that you can kill the same hero multiple times, especially when their death animation is them burning to a crisp. I think it would make more sense to have more generic heroes in the same role and sprinkle the named encounters wherever. Visually speaking I also have an issue with quickly identifying what exactly I will gain from a particular fight. I find myself needing to use the key that is provided more than I think I should after 8 hours of play, and it's not even a fully accurate key. It's missing some rewards. The cards themselves are frustrating too at times. For example there is a wind card that will generate gusts of wind on a few random rows. There is no way to see how much damage that card will do and you just have to learn that on your own. With the way the game is currently set up and having such a limited amount of time to set up a deck, I know I can't be the only one who doesn't want to guess or experiment on every run if you get a card you've never used. In short the descriptions need an overhaul. And spell check. Lastly, I beat the game with the black dragon. I guess I had expected my actual dragon to have different art depending on what dragon you played as. My dragon was not black, but red like the default. I know it's not a huge gripe, but I also don't feel like it's a big ask to have the dragon visually change depending on which you choose. I think this game has potential, but I will not be coming back for a while. It's not done baking.

As it stands right now I can't recommend this game, not because it isn't fun or anything, but because it is just too SHORT and REPETITIVE. Gameplay wise it's a good roguelite with many different combos you can set up with your elements, my only dislike is that meteor, which is a core gameplay mechanic, is a random target ability and can really screw over your runs if you go for it. Other than that, the gameplay loop is fine. Choose your path, decide what you're going to conquer, conquer regions to get bonuses, defend against bosses that try to kill you that get progressively stronger. You manage your resources, build your deck, and try to conquer things that help your build. A classic gameplay loop with the bosses all feeling mostly unique. However you're going to fight the same bosses every run with little variety. The nodes change somewhat, but each of them have a set way to deal with them. The extra run modifiers make the game harder by turning off what you're capable of doing, or making the enemy impossible to counterplay and forcing your build even further. There's very little replayability after the first run because of this, you just feel like you're in RNG hell searching for the cards for the one build that beats the high difficulty. The other thing is that after you fight the last boss of act 3, the game just ends. There's many different unique bosses to conquer on the map, and the game even teases you like there's going to be more with dialogue explaining how the knights that attack you will regroup. The other bosses just are mercenaries that try to kill you from a cutscene. The difficulty spike after the dragonslayer is immense and very jarring but when you finally beat the 3rd act... That's it. No cutscene, no fanfair, roll credits. I was enjoying myself getting in the groove, conquered several regions and was looking forwards to fighting the teased bosses and then... That's it. Run ends. Suddenly and without warning, time to start a new game. I haven't played to see if there is any secret ending or anything for defeating all the node bosses on the overworld but there's so little time I don't actually think conquering with a b-line to each overworld boss would even let you fight everything. There's not even a continue option to keep conquering the map, the run just ends after everything and it's over. All it took me is 3 runs to win the game and there's still an entire talent tree to spend on but it all feels pointless. The new cards don't add anything more than card bloat because I can already defeat everything with the base deck. It's incredibly disappointing, because I want MORE, but all I got was 3 hours worth of gameplay and another hour trying to salvage some hope that didn't come. I will recommend and change my review to recommend this game if they ever add more content, but for now there's just too little. Play the demo, you get a very similar experience and likely everything the game has to offer. Most of the game is done in the first act, the other 2 are short as hell.

A rogue lite card game where you control a dragon. After fighting armies and units, you can add new cards to decks and get various relics. Other events include destroying towns and random events where you can change your deck or make a choice. One event I encountered was reduce AP to 1 to double health. [h1] Pros: [/h1] - Pulling off different combos can be fun and interesting. - Different modifiers to increase difficulty after beating the game once. - As you play, you unlock points to use for talent tree progression. There are multiple builds to try such as whelp, fireball, etc. [h2] Suggestions: [/h2] - Add undo card button. If player mis clicks, they will be able to undo the action. - Allow player to turn off animations for bosses. Each turn, it zooms in on the boss and they show same action such as moving their hand, making the fights take longer. - Allow player to skip cut scenes. Each time you fight a raid boss, there is a cutscene you need to watch. - Show notification on screen telling the player raid will appear in next fight. There is a tracker on buttom of screen, but its easy to forget looking at it. - Change the merchant death spin to decrease the ceiling and negative effects. If you highroll, you can gain AP, gold, or strong cards. If you low roll, you can lose all your gold, take damage, or lose max HP. Visiting the merchant is worth it based on risk/reward and the results from death spin can determine if you win or lose on the run. - Add daily run with random modifiers so player can try different builds. [h3] Cons: [/h3] - Repetitive music track during fights. - Tutorial does not explain relics and could better explain combo effects with the various elements. - For each run, the raid bosses are the same. This makes the runs feel less distinct and gives the player less incentive to play the game after winning once. - Most boss fights involve summoning reinforcements and buffing them to overwhelm you or adding debuff cards to your deck. There was not much creativity when designing the bosses. - Merchants are randomly dispersed on the map. There should be at least 1 merchant location revealed so you can reliably use your gold each run. - When getting legendary or epic cards via merchant or winning fights, it should show the player the new card. Sometimes, it will not show after beating bosses. [b] Conclusion: This game is a missed opportunity. It takes 45 minutes to 1 hour to finish and each run feels similar because the raid bosses are the same. There are many aspects that can be improved including boss fights, music, and overall polish of the game. This game should be early access. It has the fundamentals of a fun game but obvious jank everywhere. There's basic bugs (sometimes rewards for fights are randomly missing), there's UI jank (cards shuffling position in your hand or other ways to encourage misclicks), there's missing quality of life (like an explanation of what almost anything is, "adds enflame to your deck" but no idea what enflame is until you play a game and find out), and then there's dubiously broken balance and flatly unfun mechanics (finishing a region adds cards to your deck that you might not want). I gave up when the Devs on discord posted about catering to the people at A36 who can now reach A40... awesome, I guess they are supporting their most hardcore players. But for someone casually trying this game I'd either wait ~6 months to see if they improve it or wait till it's 50% off. As it stands right now it's a few hours of fun and a lot of frustration.

Pros: - Great art style - Unique gameplay - Varied each playthrough - Rouge-lite mechanics keeping things fresh - Awesome music - Gambling wheel!!! Cons: - Difficult to use other cards effectively in the other dragons' decks - Rogue-lite mechanics pulling my hair out on the luck I get - Strange lag on choosing Talents, takes a few seconds for a Talent to be selected - Unbalanced encounters - Repetitive music on multiple runs - Occasional crash or lag The first thing i want to say is I really love all the dragons' designs in this game. They all are aesthetically pleasing to the eyes and are exactly what people think of when they think "Dragon Raid Boss". Being able to have so much power under your command is great. The enemies all have cool designs as well, and I like the boss mechanics that shake things up each time to try to poke holes in your dragons' weakness with their own interesting strategies. This game is a deck-building rogue-lite with a very unique mechanic system where your cards can interact with each other in various ways. I appreciate the effort that went into making the mechanics useful in some way to all 5 dragons you can play as. Each dragon has a very unique playstyle, and except the basic Fire dragon, all the dragons have unique cards in their respective decks to alter your run. Void dragon locks out other terrain and creates an army of Void Whelps to attack. Ice dragon starts off a hatchling and evolves into its powerful form later on, but doesn't take too much effort to get to the final form, and covers the terrain in ice. Thunder dragon has 2 forms that use thunder and earth spells to devastating effect. Poison dragon makes a bunch of poison terrain and can build up a lot of DoT to kill armies and single enemies fairly quickly. However, my main gripe with the game is the unique cards the other dragons have in their starting decks. They do not synergise/combo well with most of the cards you can get at random, and if you go to a shop to use the Wheel of Misfortune (Death's Wheel), you can get cards added to your deck that you don't want and can severely impact your ability to handle enemies. Oftentimes the best way to use one of the other 4 dragons is to either not use their unique cards or to ONLY use their unique cards, no in-between. That is a gross exaggeration, each dragon can make use of every card element in some way, but if you want consistent results then you will be hard-pressed to find ways to implement the cards you want to use in the various dragons' deck. I wish there were more interactions between the unique elements and the basic fire, wind, and earth cards. If there were more unique interactions, other than thunder making boulders explode for a lot of damage and wind making poison spread (sometimes? I dont quite understand it honestly), then it would be far more interesting to use the other dragons and not feel like RNG can screw up a fight if I don't draw the right cards. But even with the "sub-optimal" decks I get, I can still consistently up the difficulty on the game and still at least get to the final boss. I have beaten the final boss with every dragon, but by far the easiest dragon to use is the Fire dragon. Everything it uses can synergise with most every card to its benefit. Another issue I've had is the various raid enemies that attack the player. Most of them aren't that hard to deal with, but I've had major issues with 2 of the bosses. One requires you to use specific elements in a specific order to deal with it, but that is going to be an issue if you don't have a balance of ONLY fire, wind, and earth cards, which makes it really hard for any of the other 4 dragons to deal with that boss without taking too much damage. Using anything else has you take damage. The other boss I despise most is a boss that needs you to play a number of other card categories. If you fail to play the required number of cards in the required categories, you die in 4-5 turns, which means to beat that boss you need to have a powerful deck that lets you constantly cycle through your deck so you can consistently play every card you need to not lose to poor RNG. Going to the technical side of the game, I have discovered that there is a strange...latency? Lag? when picking a talent for your dragon. When I left-click to select a talent or right-click to deselect it, the game takes a second or 2 to process it and then does as I request. And after I had beaten the final boss for the first time and went to continue to total domination, I had to get off for the night. The next morning I tried to continue my save but discovered the game would crash upon loading it, which forced me to forego the whole run and start all over on a new dragon. Another issue is the UI, it is obtuse and can get in the way. When selecting a card, you must click and drag the card to the space you wish to play it on, but oftentimes selecting the right card can be a hassle if you have a large hand size. Parts of the UI on the right side also cover a little of the battlefield - and while you can easily toggle the on the right side to not see the attacks the boss or hero will do, it is a minor annoyance to not easily see both the enemy cards being played and see enemy type/health bar. All in all, a good game for its price, and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys deck-building games or rouge-lites. I have high hopes for the devs to continue improving upon the game and making it the best it can be.

I am writing this from a perspective of someone who really enjoyed the game and finished it as all 5 dragon aspects on max difficulty lvl. It is an awesome block puzzle/card game dark fantasy Slay The Spire combo. Great core mechanics idea. Unfortunately the quantity and quality of content makes this position look like a very undercooked product. A game in this state should still be in beta - I hope that the revenue from selling this as a finished game will actually fuel further development because there is a ton of potential that I would love to see unfolded. Key offenders: - Very few talent choices, even fewer that impact the game in a meaningful way. - Most cards actually make your deck worse for adding them - the further they go from the few basic, cheap cantrips that interact with the core elemental mechanic, the worse. - Despite the mostly poor/unimpactful skill tree, if the core mechanics are grasped, the game is boringly easy to steamroll - and it does not really matter much what you put in your deck. With the exception of enabling the armament that permanently locks out the "Boss Mechanics" after a short period use. A really meaningful and interesting difficulty spike, but it just amplifies the glaringness of previous points. I wish this game well and will be happy to revisit after some much needed overhauls. It was worth the $ though.

I am giving this a negative review, despite genuinely loving the core concept. In its current state, this game should never have been released. It is painfully clear that the developer pushed it out before it was finished. The experience is marred by several glaring issues: Technical Polish: The game is riddled with annoying bugs and a clunky UI. Poor Design: Tooltip design is subpar, and many mechanics are either left unexplained or are fundamentally broken. Information Accessibility: You cannot view your armament modifiers during a run—a major oversight. UI Obstruction: Units occasionally get hidden behind UI elements that cannot be toggled off. In a game where strategic planning is paramount, being unable to see the board is a dealbreaker. The Absolute Dealbreaker The worst part—and that would be reason enough for a negative rating, even without the other aspects—is that the game simply dies at the finish line. After hours of careful play and surviving multiple difficulty modifiers, defeating the final boss (Armament) often results in a soft lock. The enemies are dead, but the battle never concludes, regardless of how many times you pass your turn. You are forced to quit, losing hours of progress at the moment of victory. Even when I managed to bypass that bug and reach the "Conquer the World" phase, the game eventually hung mid-run, forcing another hard reset. Another campaign ends and I am forced to begin a new game. Honestly, it feels borderline evil to release a game with game-breaking bugs that only trigger after a player has invested hours of their time.

I've noticed the lack of reviews that were backed by fair amount of playtime, I'll scribble my own things down now that I've completed the game entirely In the shortest form NSI is a niche rogueli-k-t-e deckbuilder that requires field management aside from the deck, this alone is what makes it feel different than other roguelike deckbuilders Generally gameplay representation looks a lot different from any other by design choice, for example you conquer some map regions in this to progress, and every X fights intervals you face a core boss, but technically it's actually pretty same with any other deckbuilder mapping system, just visually served differently, I think it was a nice change of pace. You begin your runs as a big bad dragon with massive health pool and absurd damaging cards, you have limited healing sources throughout your run and your goal is to refine your deck and maybe get some relics before facing the last boss to conclude the run, this part is pretty familiar, right? Then comes the field management system. It's not mandatory to play into this, but I can easily say this is the intended way to play the game. There are some elements, each dragon (there are multiple!) has some extra unique element too, and whenever you cast your abilities on any portions of your battle field, you leave traces of these elements, and when multiple elements are merged magic happens, be it shielding, area damage, poison, burn, you get it. Playing in this fashion, it requires more of the active 'thinking' as you are required to keep up your management during the fights (this may feel overwhelming to some) and more often than not it'll be you instead of rng that decides the fate of your encounters. Now the cons: Can get buggy at times, it's not horrible, but can be annoying time to time There are several 'cheese' builds you can follow, these will likely trivialize the need of field management part of the game Meta-progression is a necessity to use in order to succeed in higher difficulties Overall it's a nice and different game, if you are one of roguelike deckbuilder addicts, you should give it a go, but be warned, field management requires active thinking so it might not click with everyone

Completely embarrassing to call this a finished product. Visual design looks generic, to the tune of those early 2k's flash games with one actual character design surrounded by half-assed enemy units. It looks second rate even by mobile game standards. For some reason the unstylized menu text in the settings was hazy and pixelated even after adjusting my resolution, making it hard for me to read even with my glasses. Sound design is flat and uninteresting, and I only actually noticed three different songs (one of which was generic soft angelic choir crap as a boss fight theme). The game was also completely muted on first boot for some reason, which technically isn't a *problem*, but it's bizarre. The terrain manipulation and grid-targeting mechanics made my hopes much higher than they should have been for the combat, where it's very clear that almost all of those mechanics are completely irrelevant unless you get specific, sometimes multiple relics to enhance them. Even then, the relics are very badly balanced and I found myself struggling to activate some of them for completely mediocre effects while others activated completely automatically every turn and outright wiped the field for me. The random-target cards like Sirocco and Meteor Storm sounded fun until the seventh time in a row that they hit absolutely nothing on a field that's halfway full of enemies, and several cards simply won't perform the elemental interactions they're seemingly supposed to. Other cards simply don't tell you all of their effects, like Pyroblast having a base attack value despite the card text only saying that it does an amount of damage per lava tile. It's so blatantly clear what the "right" cards, abilities and items are to pick when you've seen a few already, and that creates the effect where you either struggle to get through normal encounters with careful decisions, or you easily breeze through even without a synergistic build or good draws just because your relics/boss abilities are that strong. Worst of all, the bugs in this game are downright shameful. My Rage meter was missing from the start of my first run after I got out of the (bad) tutorial that told me how it's used, and I optimistically assumed that it was just not unlocked yet because I wasn't far enough in the game. But no, that's a known bug; a core game mechanic that other mechanics interact with, completely gone with no explanation like someone had just cropped it out of the UI in MS Paint. You can't have a math-driven, thoughtful deckbuilding game where basic features just refuse to function and where important functions/definitions are obscured from the player! I got this game in a bundle for less than two dollars proportionally, and I still wish I could refund it. Find another game; there's a billion in this genre that meet their design goals better than this one.

I want you to imagine someone came up to you and said, "Here's a finished product." And you looked at it, and it was a sandwich with no bread. Just a bloke holding some ham, going "that'll be ten quid." That's this game. That's what we're dealing with. Let's start with the visuals, because apparently nobody else did. It looks like an early-2000s Flash game — you remember those, you played them at work when you should've been doing your job — except those were free, and made by one teenager in Ohio, and they had an excuse. Now the combat. This is the tragic bit, because the ideas are genuinely there - terrain manipulation, grid targeting, elemental interactions. Lovely. On paper. In practice, almost none of it matters unless you've collected the specific relics that switch the mechanics on, like the game's core features are DLC you pay for in luck. And the relics themselves are balanced like a seesaw with an elephant on one end. Some of them I couldn't activate if my life depended on it, for effects that wouldn't scare a pigeon. Others activated automatically every single turn and wiped the entire field while I sat there doing sudoku. And the bugs. Oh, the bugs. My Rage meter - a core mechanic, the tutorial teaches you about it, other systems interact with it - just wasn't there. Gone. Cropped out of the UI like someone did it in MS Paint on their lunch break. I assumed I hadn't unlocked it yet, because I'm an optimist, which was my mistake. It's a known bug. It's a decent proof of concept wearing a full-release costume. There are a billion games in this genre that actually meet their own design goals. Go find one of those. This one's still finding itself.

A solid blend of stealth and action. The tension of sneaking past enemies is thrilling, and the mechanics are smooth. Some areas feel repetitive, but overall, it’s a fun challenge.
The tension is real! Every mission feels like a puzzle, and the sense of accomplishment when you clear an area undetected is unmatched.
The difficulty can be unforgiving, but that’s what makes it so satisfying. Once you master stealth, you feel unstoppable.
Every level gives you multiple ways to approach it. Whether you want to be a ghost or take out enemies quietly, it’s up to you.
If you love sneaking through enemy bases and outsmarting guards, this is for you. It’s all about strategy and execution.
I’ve tried going for a pacifist run and an aggressive run—both felt completely different, which shows the game’s flexibility.
The atmosphere is so well done. The environments feel tense, and the background music adds to the immersion.
The more you play, the more you appreciate how well-designed the levels are. They really make you think.
Reminds me of the stealth sections from old-school Metal Gear games, but with more freedom in approach.
I love how it forces you to be patient. Running in without a plan always ends in disaster, and that’s a good thing.
The fact that there’s no hand-holding makes it even better. You have to figure things out on your own, which is rare these days.
Every enemy encounter feels like a puzzle. You have to observe their movements and plan accordingly.
The mechanics are simple to understand but hard to master. That’s what makes it so engaging.
I keep coming back to it because no two playthroughs feel exactly the same. There’s always something new to try.
